newsitem.title: KENYA: Sufficient aid for Zaire sits waiting, unusable.
newsitem.headline: Sufficient aid for Zaire sits waiting, unusable.

text.p: Aid agencies used to begging rich countries for food, medicines and shelter say that for once they already have all they need to save a million refugees in Zaire.
But none of it will help unless local or foreign politicians clear the way, and meanwhile the refugees are dying.
A front line separates the missing people from the supplies that could save them and there are no signs that swift foreign intervention will change this.

"The good thing, if one can say that, about emergencies in an area of emergencies is that we already have the supplies we need for immediate operations," said Brenda Barton of the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP).

No huge aid airlift from Europe or other far-off places, as in 1994 when Rwanda's genocide triggered a mass exodus, is likely to be needed if intervention or a ceasefire opens routes to 1.2 million Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees.
After wars in Sudan, Somalia, Ethiopia, Rwanda and Burundi, East Africa has an aid infrastructure second to none.
It even bolsters the economies of stabler countries such as Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania where much of the aid is stockpiled.
Barton said the WFP had food to feed as many as 2.3 million people for two months in stores in neighbouring countries.
Other aid agencies have plentiful stocks of other supplies.

Under contingency plans, waiting desperately for a green light, aid would be trucked into Zaire over the border from well-stocked Rwanda and flown in by Hercules aircraft to Bukavu and Goma towns from the regional Kenyan hub, Nairobi.
Maize flour, beans, oil and salt, water tanks and chlorine, plastic sheeting for shelter, blankets and medicines are top of the list for the refugees who have fled their camps.
Lost from view and without help for up to three weeks, they are believed to have scattered in the mountains and jungle of eastern Zaire, an inhospitable area with few roads.

Andrew Hunt of Christian Aid, who flew over much of anarchic eastern Zaire this week, said terrified villagers even hundreds of km (miles) from the fighting had fled to the bush for safety, sending higher the number of people on the run.
The further west the refugees flee, away from aid workers and supplies waiting in Rwanda, Burundi, Uganda and Tanzania, the harder they will be to reach in any rescue mission.
"That is one of the worst areas in the world to mount a relief effort," Andrew Hall of the IFRC Red Cross federation said of a region of volcanic rock, dense jungle and few roads.
He said the Swedish military was sending the IFRC two Hercules aircraft to Nairobi, where a third could be chartered from a local company, Southern Air Services, if needed.
Refugees are already dying of thirst in the harsh mountains, say Zaireans who have fled into Rwanda, where Hutus dare not go.

Some 40,000 refugees -- a drop in the ocean -- have poured into neighbouring states better equipped to care for them. Most are Zaireans, who have now become the third group of refugees after the Hutus of Rwanda and Burundi.
As often, the obstacles to aid are political. Zaire, tired of its destabilising refugee burden, wants them out and has told aid workers they may not feed them in Zaire.
Tutsi-led Rwanda, which wants innocent Hutus to come home, will only let enough aid through its territory to enable the refugees to recover their strength and start the journey home.
The key to the problem is the guilty -- Rwandan Hutu rebels who led the 1994 genocide that killed some 800,000 Tutsis.
Still armed, they have controlled the refugees for more than two years, using camps as bases for military strikes, and will not go home to face the wrath of the Tutsis who survived.

No one knows how the Rwandan Hutu fighters will extricate themselves from their current predicament. Zairean rebels including Tutsis allied to Rwanda have driven them from border camps, but they have nowhere to go.
